column3:
This sheet shows the mapping of cornerstone indicators from the Future Streets Oxfordshire project, against the themes and factors that emerged from workshop 1 and 2
✓✓  = Strong and direct association with factor 
✓ = Factor is implied in the indicator

Under the tick marks, each bullet point is a verbatim response from workshops 1 and 2 that relates to the indicator.
NOTE: Not all of the mapped responses were used while creating the indicator, but were mapped retrospectively to see the breadth covered by the indicator.

column2: Theme
Factors

column3: People value streets that are quiet enough to bump into neighbours, talk and let children play outside. Chance encounters and accidental contact between neighbours make a street feel like a community rather than just a road.
column4:
1. People want places to gather that are free, welcoming and easy to walk into: community cafes, third spaces and community centres that function as neighbourhood living rooms. These spaces matter for everyone, and especially for young people, elderly residents and anyone who needs somewhere to be among people. 

2. People value outdoor spaces designed for spending time in: benches in the shade, open and unlocked parks, squares with planting and room to sit and play. People imagine streets and public spaces where you can stop, rest and be among people freely.
column5: Street parties, fetes, BBQs and local festivals are the moments when community becomes real and visible: diverse food, people mixing across cultures, belonging felt in a single afternoon. People across Oxfordshire want these rituals everywhere, not just in areas where the confidence or resource already exists to make them happen.
column6: People value streets where everyone can be present: across cultures, backgrounds, ages and beliefs. Multicultural diversity makes neighbourhoods stronger. People say directly and without softening that racism and intimidation have no place in their streets, and that welcome should be real for everyone.
column7: People value streets and spaces where children can play freely outdoors: in parks, on pavements, in cul-de-sacs and town centres. Well-maintained, welcoming play spaces matter for every neighbourhood, and children playing outside together signals streets that feel safe and alive for everyone.
column8: People value the networks that connect generations and keep people from being isolated: youth groups, community groups that support elderly residents, and the informal ties that sustain people through hard times. Neighbourhoods where young and old share spaces and activities, and where no one is left on their own, feel fundamentally healthier.
column9: 1. People value streets and public spaces that work for everyone, whatever their mobility needs: dropped kerbs, smooth surfaces, step-free access and room for scooters and wheelchairs. Accessible infrastructure should be the standard across all of Oxfordshire, not something concentrated in central Oxford. 2. People value pavements that are smooth, wide enough to walk comfortably and easy to cross: well-maintained surfaces, more crossing points and places to rest along the way. Streets designed for people on foot, with seating, shelter and room to move, make everyday life possible for everyone.
column10: 1. People value public transport that is frequent, reliable and genuinely connected across Oxfordshire: buses that run between towns, trains that work, and a unified system that doesn't require a car to fill the gaps. The aspiration is transport good enough to be a real choice for everyone. 2. People want public transport to be affordable for everyone, and free public transport appears repeatedly as a genuine aspiration: as an ecological good, a matter of equity and a practical necessity for people who cannot afford taxis or car ownership. Losing even a single bus route has real consequences for those who depend on it most.
column11: People value the freedom to reach the things that make daily life possible: food shops, doctors, jobs and each other. Good connectivity matters for everyone, and uneven access, within areas as much as between them, falls hardest on elderly residents, young people and families who depend on it most.
column12: 1. People value cycling and walking infrastructure that is safe, connected and usable for everyday journeys: between villages and towns, not just within them. For people who cannot afford a car and for children making their way to school, good walking and cycling routes that work for all ages and all types of bikes represent genuine freedom of movement. 2. Secure bike parking matters as much as the routes themselves. People want to park a bike in town easily and safely, with space for cargo bikes and different bike types, so that cycling — alongside walking and wheeling — works as a practical choice for everyone.
column13: People value streets where space belongs to everyone: pavements clear of parked cars, room to walk and cycle, and public spaces designed for people rather than vehicle storage. People want streets progressively reclaimed for human life, from smarter parking management to fully pedestrianised town centres.
column14:
1. People want green woven into the street itself: trees on every street, planting in pavements and window boxes, green walls and concrete replaced with plants and flowers. The vision is of streets alive with growing things, not grey with tarmac and hard surfaces. 

2. People value open green spaces that are well-maintained, genuinely inviting and accessible to everyone: parks, fields and nature shortcuts that don't run alongside busy roads. Protecting those spaces from development for housing and car parking is part of the same vision.
column15: People value old trees, hedgerows, wild verges and the presence of birds and wildlife as part of what makes streets worth living in. People imagine streets and public spaces designed for other species as much as for people: meadows instead of manicured lawns, buildings with swift bricks and bat boxes, and lighting that serves wildlife and keeps people safe.
column16:
1. People value streets and green spaces that are genuinely cared for and free from chemicals that harm ecological life: maintained verges, protected trees, pesticide-free towns and no chemical spraying. Collective stewardship that involves communities, from village litter picks to protecting and nurturing newly planted trees, is part of the same vision. 

2. People imagine streets and shared spaces where food is actively grown by communities: window pots of herbs, community allotments, food crops in the streets and food growing woven into school life. Growing food together connects ecological stewardship to community life and food security.
column17: People value streets and neighbourhoods designed to work with water and climate: good drainage that prevents flooding, rainwater captured and reused, waterways kept clean. People imagine streets and buildings that generate their own energy and manage heat, from solar panels and grey water recycling to reinstating the historical features that kept buildings cool.
column18:
1. People value streets where traffic moves at human speeds: where children can cross safely, people can walk without fear, and the volume and speed of cars, delivery vehicles and fast electric bikes don't dominate street life. When streets feel safe from traffic, people walk, cycle and spend time outside. 

2. People value streets that feel safe for everyone at all times: free from harassment and the fear of crime, well-lit and welcoming after dark. Free and accessible leisure centres and outdoor gyms matter especially for people with health conditions and those who cannot travel far.
column19:
1. People value clean air as a basic condition of healthy street life: free from traffic fumes, smog and the pollution of diesel and petrol engines. Trees, cleaner buses and the shift away from fossil fuel vehicles are part of the vision for streets where air quality supports, rather than undermines, health. 

2. People value clean air as something everyone should benefit from equally. Traffic reduction schemes that deliver cleaner streets to wealthier neighbourhoods while displacing pollution to main roads and council estates fall short of that vision.
column20:
1. People share a recognition that streets designed well can actively support mental wellbeing: quiet enough to hear birdsong, lit by natural light and with places to sit, slow down and reflect. The sensory quality of a street, its pace, its sounds and its light, shapes how people feel. 

2. People value streets that are clean, uncluttered and well-maintained: free from litter, excessive bins, urban furniture and visual mess. A clean and well-kept street matters for everyone, and people note that litter and neglect are worse in areas outside central Oxford.
column21:
1. People value neighbourhoods with a diverse range of locally-owned, independent shops, cafes, restaurants and services where the basics of daily life, including food, can be sourced locally. Business rates, community ownership and local economic structures that help independents thrive are part of the vision. 

2. Access to basic shops and services matters for everyone. In some areas of Oxfordshire, people describe expensive convenience stores, no cash machine and limited local options as everyday realities: the vision is of neighbourhoods where essential shops, especially food, are accessible to all.
column22:
1. People value neighbourhoods that feel alive and locally owned: places with buoyancy and vibrancy, not hollowed out by betting shops, vape stores and outlets that serve no one's community. Whose story a place tells matters too: public spaces and heritage that reflect the full diversity of the people who live there. 

2. People value the distinctiveness that makes each place feel irreplaceable: historic buildings, Victorian conservation areas, garden walls that hold the memory of older landscapes and streets that tell a local story. Pride of place and beauty in the built environment, old and new, matter deeply.
column23: 1. People value the ability to stay in the communities they belong to: affordable rents, social housing and housing costs that don't force people out of the neighbourhoods they have built their lives in. Living near where you work, and keeping communities intact across income levels, is part of what holds them together. 2. People value economic security as a foundation of neighbourhood health: freedom from reliance on food banks, wages that cover the cost of living and an end to the structural poverty that shapes daily life for many in Oxfordshire. The voluntary sector that supports communities deserves affordable, accessible locations too.
column24: People imagine streets and public spaces that are creative, playful and culturally alive: murals, street art, exhibition spaces, workshops and music at bus stops. Libraries in bus stops, repair spaces in old banks and land schools for shared skills all point to a vision of streets as places where culture happens and communities learn together.
column25:
1. People value civic participation that genuinely reaches everyone: young people, less connected residents and communities whose voices have rarely shaped decisions. Civic education in schools, proactive outreach and knowing how to navigate the system are part of how that becomes real. 

2. People value governance that is proactive, collaborative and trustworthy: councils that ask communities what they need rather than waiting for complaints, and organisations that work together rather than in isolated pockets. The quality of the relationship between communities and local government is seen as a foundation of neighbourhood health.
column26: 1. People value the knowledge and wisdom that local communities hold about their own neighbourhoods, and want that to drive decisions. A different kind of revitalisation is possible: one that centres local people rather than outside professionals who arrive and co-opt what communities are already doing. 2. People imagine communities with meaningful control over funding, local places and the decisions that shape their streets. Hyper-local democratic structures, community-owned budgets and networks of local organisations run by local people are part of that vision.
column27: People value local government with the capacity to plan long-term, coordinate across departments and act on a shared vision for streets and neighbourhoods. Adequate funding, protection of public assets like school grounds and land, and genuinely joined-up thinking across organisations are what good governance looks like.
column28: 1. People value shared responsibility for the places they live in: caring for shared spaces, respecting rules that benefit everyone and treating each other with consideration. 2. People see a drift toward individualism, entitlement and reduced care for shared spaces as something that corrodes neighbourhood life from the inside. Designing streets that make cooperative behaviour natural, and nurturing cultures of collective responsibility rather than individual convenience, are part of the vision.
